summary: Specifies PB-TNC, a posture broker protocol identical to the Trusted Computing Group's IF-TNCCS 2.0. It carries posture information between a device and a network and is evaluated against the Network Endpoint Assessment requirements. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: A messenger carries a device's health answers to the front desk and brings back the decision, and this describes how the messenger talks.

questions: what is a posture broker protocol
what are the pb-tnc batch types
subtitle: How a device and a network server swap health-check messages in batches before deciding whether the device may join.

tldr.problem: Before a device is let onto a network, the network may want to check its health (patches, anti-virus and so on). That needs a common way to carry the checks between the device and the server and to manage the assessment.
tldr.mechanism: PB-TNC wraps posture messages in compact binary batches of type-length-value messages. The client and server take turns sending batches, a small state machine controls the session, and the server ends with a result and an access recommendation.
tldr.outcome: PB-TNC is identical to the Trusted Computing Group's IF-TNCCS 2.0 and is checked against the NEA requirements. It relies on the transport underneath for security, and the RFC is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 5793 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2010, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the IETF specification of the TNC IF-TNCCS 2.0 posture broker protocol.

sections.title: What PB-TNC Is For
sections.content:
RFC 5793 specifies PB-TNC, a Posture Broker (PB) protocol identical to the Trusted Computing Group's IF-TNCCS 2.0 protocol. It then evaluates PB-TNC against the requirements in the Network Endpoint Assessment (NEA) requirements specification, RFC 5209. It does not define an architecture; it defines a protocol that works within the reference model in that document.

The main job of PB-TNC is to carry Posture Attribute (PA) messages between Posture Collectors on the endpoint and Posture Validators on the server. It also carries its own messages between the Posture Broker Client and the Posture Broker Server and manages the state of the assessment.
sections.eli5: Before a laptop joins a network, someone has to ask it health questions. PB-TNC is the set of rules for passing those questions and answers back and forth.

sections.title: Addressing and Design Choices
sections.content:
Each PA message has a message type made of a PA Message Vendor ID and a PA subtype. A Posture Validator can say which types it wants, and the broker delivers matching messages, so collectors need not know which validators are installed. Vendor ID 0 means a value registered with IANA and defined in an RFC; a non-zero vendor ID is a Private Enterprise Number and the vendor defines the values.

PB-TNC also supports dynamic identifiers. When the server loads a Posture Validator it assigns it a Posture Validator ID, and a collector can reply to just that validator. Static identifiers were considered and rejected because they make a brittle system.

For efficiency, the format is binary with a Type-Length-Value (TLV) structure, chosen to suit low bandwidth transports and low power devices.
sections.eli5: Each message has a label saying what kind it is, so the mail goes to the right desk. If you want to answer one particular person, you can use the name tag they gave you.

sections.title: Batches and the Session State Machine
sections.content:
PB-TNC carries batches of messages between a Posture Broker Client and a Posture Broker Server. To work over half-duplex transports such as those based on EAP, the two sides take turns sending a single batch. Full-duplex operation is also supported so an exchange can be restarted at once, for example when server policy changes.

A session starts in the Init state. A client that opened the transport connection sends a CDATA batch; a server that opened it sends SDATA. They then alternate. When the server sends a RESULT batch the session moves to the Decided state, which is not terminal. The client can send CRETRY to restart an exchange, and over a full-duplex transport the server can send SRETRY. A CLOSE batch, or the transport closing, leads to the End state.

Both sides MUST follow this state machine. With a half-duplex transport the server cannot send SRETRY in the Decided state, so it should close the connection without a CLOSE batch and start a new session.

PB-TNC relies on the Posture Transport (PT) protocol for security: PT MUST support mutual authentication, confidentiality and integrity protection, and replay protection. The RFC adds requirements PT-6 to PT-9, such as being connection oriented and able to carry binary data.
sections.eli5: It is like a walkie-talkie where you take turns. The device talks, then the server, until the server says its decision. Either side can later ask to start over, or hang up.

sections.title: Batch Header and Message Format
sections.content:
Every batch starts with one header, followed by zero or more messages. The header holds an 8-bit Version (MUST be 2), a 1-bit Directionality flag (0 from a client, 1 from a server), 19 reserved bits, a 4-bit Batch Type and a 32-bit Batch Length that is at least 8.

The batch types are CDATA (1), SDATA (2), RESULT (3), CRETRY (4), SRETRY (5) and CLOSE (6). A batch type not allowed in the current state gets a fatal Unexpected Batch Type error in a CLOSE batch.

Each message has a Flags byte, a 24-bit PB-TNC Vendor ID, a 32-bit Message Type, a 32-bit Message Length (at least 12) and a value. The NOSKIP flag says whether a recipient may skip a message it does not understand. If it is set and the message cannot be processed, the recipient MUST NOT act on the batch and answers with a fatal Unsupported Mandatory Message error. Vendor ID 0xffffff and type 0xffffffff are reserved.
sections.eli5: A batch is an envelope with a short label on the front, and inside are smaller notes that each have their own label. A note marked must-read cannot be thrown away.

sections.title: The Standard Message Types
sections.content:
Eight IETF standard message types exist, all used with vendor ID 0. PB-PA (1) carries one PA message plus routing information; every implementation MUST support it and its NOSKIP flag MUST be set. Its EXCL flag asks for delivery only to the identified collector or validator, using 16-bit identifiers where 0xffff is reserved.

The server sends PB-Assessment-Result (2), a value from 0 (compliant) to 4 (unable to determine from the attributes provided), in every RESULT batch. It may add PB-Access-Recommendation (3) with code 1 for Access Allowed, 2 for Access Denied or 3 for Quarantined. That recommendation is not authoritative; access control systems typically use other information too.

PB-Remediation-Parameters (4) carries a Remediation-URI (type 1) or Remediation-String (type 2). PB-Language-Preference (6) carries an Accept-Language value. PB-Reason-String (7) gives a human-readable reason for the decision. PB-Experimental (0) MUST NOT be used in production.
sections.eli5: There are a few kinds of notes: a note carrying the health questions, a grade (fine, a little off, very off), a verdict (come in, stay out, wait in the lobby), and tips for fixing problems.

sections.title: PB-Error and Error Codes
sections.content:
PB-Error (5) reports problems and every implementation MUST implement it. Its FATAL flag decides what happens: if set, the sender terminates the exchange after sending the error in a CLOSE batch and the recipient terminates the session. An error raised while processing a PB-Error MUST be fatal, which prevents an infinite loop of errors.

The standard error codes are 0 Unexpected Batch Type, 1 Invalid Parameter, 2 Local Error, 3 Unsupported Mandatory Message and 4 Version Not Supported. Codes 1 and 3 carry the offset of the offending value or message. Version Not Supported carries Bad, Max and Min version fields and MUST be the only message in a CLOSE batch with version 2, so version negotiation can always work.
sections.eli5: If something goes wrong, a side can send a note saying what. For serious problems it says so and hangs up, so two confused machines do not keep yelling at each other.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
PT is required and assumed to provide authentication, confidentiality, integrity protection and replay protection. The RFC still lists the threats: untrusted intermediaries that observe, modify, reorder, replay, truncate or block the exchange, and compromised trusted parties such as the Posture Transport Client and Server. The consequences it names include wrong assessment decisions, harmful remediation instructions and denial of network access.

The main countermeasure is the security of the PT protocol. NEA servers should be built like AAA servers, should be robust against hostile clients, and clients should not blindly follow remediation instructions, validating dangerous actions such as patches, for instance by asking the user.
sections.eli5: The protocol trusts the road it travels on to be safe. The RFC warns that bad people on the road, or a crooked front desk, could cause trouble, so the device should double-check before doing anything risky.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
The RFC creates four IANA registries: PB-TNC Message Types, PA Subtypes, PB-TNC Remediation Parameters Types and PB-TNC Error Codes. New values are added by Expert Review with Specification Required. Values must be documented in a permanently and publicly available specification, and IETF standard values must also be useful and clear enough to ensure interoperability.

The message type, remediation type and error code registries start with the values this RFC defines. The PA Subtypes registry starts empty, and later RFCs such as PA-TNC fill it. Assessment Result and Access Recommendation values need no registry because changing them requires a new PB-TNC version number.
sections.eli5: There are official lists of the labels in use. Anyone adding to a list must write down what the label means where everyone can read it.

fields.name: D
fields.desc: Directionality: 0 from a client, 1 from a server.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to 0 on transmission, ignored on reception.

fields.name: B-Type
fields.desc: Batch type that drives the state machine.

fields.name: Batch Length
fields.desc: Size of the full batch in octets; at least 8.
